platforms.title: Cataract Signs: When New Glasses Still Don't Fix It
platforms.meta_description: Halos around headlights at night and glasses that never quite work are classic early cataract signs, different from an ordinary vision change.
platforms.body_html:
Getting new glasses and still not seeing clearly afterward is a specific pattern worth paying close attention to. According to the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) and Cleveland Clinic, one of the more overlooked early cataract signs is exactly this: frequent prescription changes that never quite restore sharp vision, unlike an ordinary refractive change that a new lens fixes cleanly.

Why Headlights Suddenly Look Like Starbursts

The other hallmark sign shows up specifically at night. The AAO describes glare and halos around lights — oncoming headlights or streetlights that seem to spread into a bright ring — as a classic cataract symptom, distinct from simple night-vision decline. This happens because the clouding lens scatters incoming light instead of focusing it cleanly, and it's often the reason night driving starts to feel unexpectedly stressful before daytime vision changes much at all.

Two Signs That Don't Mean the Same Thing

It's worth distinguishing this from presbyopia (the common, expected loss of close-up focus with age, fixed reliably by reading glasses) and from a one-time prescription update after a stable eye. The AAO notes that some people even temporarily read better without reading glasses as an early cataract effect on the lens's focusing power — a change that feels like an improvement but is actually part of the same process.

What to Actually Do About It

Neither symptom on its own means surgery is needed immediately. The AAO notes that when cataract symptoms are mild, an updated prescription can be enough for a while — surgery becomes the recommended option once cataracts start interfering with daily tasks like driving, reading, or seeing well at night, not based on a specific vision-chart number alone. That's a decision made with an eye doctor based on how much daily function is affected, not a fixed threshold.

What Actually Happens at the Exam

A routine dilated eye exam is what actually confirms a cataract — eye drops widen the pupil so the doctor can see the lens directly with specialized equipment, rather than guessing from symptoms alone. This is also the same visit where other causes of glare or blurred vision, like dry eye or an early prescription mismatch, get ruled out, so the appointment does more than confirm one suspicion — it also maps out how quickly the lens is changing, which shapes how soon a follow-up exam is needed.

When to Book an Eye Exam

If night driving has started to feel harder specifically because of glare rather than general dimness, or if a new glasses prescription hasn't restored the clarity it used to, that combination is worth describing to an eye doctor directly, rather than waiting to see if it resolves on its own — those two details narrow down the cause faster than "my vision is blurry" alone.

Next time you pick up a new pair of glasses, pay attention to whether the clarity actually holds over time — if it fades again within just a few months, that specific detail is what's worth mentioning at your next eye appointment.
